section_summary: This section documents the political crisis and reconstruction of Prince Fumimaro Konoye's Cabinet in Japan between May and July 1938, alongside earlier reviews of the 1937 wartime mobilization. It details the internal Cabinet cleavage over the prosecution of the war in China, resulting in the appointment of Generals Kazushige Ugaki, Sadao Araki, and Seishiro Itagaki, and business leader Seishin Ikeda, aimed at consolidating continental policy and breaking the military impasse. In response, the United States State Department formulated comprehensive instructions and desiderata to protect American treaty rights, missionary and commercial interests, and the Open Door policy in China, culminating in Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's formal representations to Foreign Minister Ugaki.

subfiles.about: Analyzes the impact of the outbreak of Sino-Japanese hostilities in July 1937 on Japanese domestic politics, the Diet's legislative support, and the establishment of Imperial Headquarters.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Concluding part of Grew's annual 1937 review: party friction submerged in the war effort, extraordinary Diet sessions, Imperial Headquarters created, and parliamentary party politics effectively collapsed.
subfiles.title: Annual Review of Political Affairs in Japan for 1937 (Domestic Politics Section)

subfiles.about: Summarizes and comments upon Ambassador Grew's analysis of internal disunity in the Japanese Cabinet over China policy.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 2912: Konoye favored an elastic strategy to end the China war quickly; the Army sought limited pressure while husbanding resources against Russia. Operations will intensify.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 2912

subfiles.about: Provides an extensive evaluation of internal dissension within the Japanese Cabinet over the prosecution of the China conflict and national mobilization.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew evaluates the political tensions within the Japanese Cabinet precipitated by military reverses in southern Shantung and Prince Konoye's contemplation of resignation. He contrasts the strategic views of Konoye's civilian circle with those of War Minister Sugiyama and Imperial Headquarters, explaining the Army's reluctance to overextend while facing the Soviet Union. The despatch reports that following consultations with Prince Saionji, Konoye agreed to remain in office after reaching a compromise with the military for more vigorous operations, including a projected advance on Hankow.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2912: 'Political Situation in Japan'

subfiles.about: Reports confidential information indicating an impending Cabinet reshuffle to meet demands for a more vigorous prosecution of the China war.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew relays a friend of Konoe: cabinet to be reconstituted for more aggressive warfare; Ugaki to replace Hirota. The Asahi edition reporting it was censored.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 330 Regarding Impending Cabinet Reconstitution

subfiles.about: Presents a strictly confidential paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 330 concerning impending Japanese Cabinet changes.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 330: Hirota to be replaced by Ugaki, Hiranuma possible adviser, Konoe remains premier; an Asahi edition was censored.
subfiles.title: Department of State Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 330

subfiles.about: Announces the official ministerial appointments of General Ugaki, Seishin Ikeda, and General Araki to the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew announces May 26, 1938 appointments: Ugaki Foreign Minister, Ikeda Finance and Commerce and Industry, Araki Education.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 332 Announcing Cabinet Appointments

subfiles.about: Transmits an undated duplicate text reporting the Cabinet appointments of Ugaki, Ikeda, and Araki.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (unsigned)
subfiles.summary: Unsigned duplicate telegram, received May 26, 1938, announcing Ugaki as Foreign Minister, Ikeda for Finance and Commerce, Araki for Education.
subfiles.title: Duplicate Tokyo Telegram Announcing Cabinet Appointments

subfiles.about: Analyzes the factional balance and strategic significance of the newly reconstructed Konoye Cabinet following the victory at Hsuchow.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew analyzes the reshuffle as a victory for Konoye's forceful faction over Sugiyama, delayed until the Hsuchow victory. Ugaki and Ikeda balance moderates and business; Araki satisfies nationalists; Hirota was bewildered.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 333: Analysis of Cabinet Reconstruction

subfiles.about: Provides additional details on impending changes in the War Ministry and clarifies former Foreign Minister Hirota's political alignments.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Sugiyama and Umezu to be replaced by Itagaki and Tojo; Hirota was tied to Sugiyama's faction. Assesses Ikeda's economic controls and Ugaki as likely future premier.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 335: Further Intelligence on Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Paraphrases Tokyo Telegram No. 335 concerning the realignment of Hirota, the War Ministry changes, and the roles of Ugaki and Ikeda.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 335: Hirota lost office through ties to Sugiyama; Itagaki and Tojo to enter the War Ministry; Ugaki and Ikeda assessed.
subfiles.title: Department of State Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 335

subfiles.about: Announces the official appointment of General Seishiro Itagaki as Minister of War succeeding General Sugiyama.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew announces General Seishiro Itagaki's appointment as Minister of War on June 3, 1938, after Sugiyama's resignation.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 352 Announcing General Itagaki as Minister of War

subfiles.about: Summarizes British press reactions to the Japanese Cabinet reorganization reported in London Despatch No. 430.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Notes British press views of the Japanese cabinet changes: The Times saw militarists fighting to a finish; the Manchester Guardian said the military had conquered Japan.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on London Despatch No. 430

subfiles.about: Reports British editorial opinion on the Japanese Cabinet changes, the dispute over the Chinese Affairs Bureau, and the Battle of Hsuchow.
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, Counselor of Embassy, London
subfiles.summary: Counselor Johnson reports London press views of the Cabinet changes as a move toward military fascism and greater belligerence; the Guardian foresees an unwinnable protracted war.
subfiles.title: London Despatch No. 430: British Press Comment on Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Analyzes and critiques a Soviet press commentary from the Pacific Star on internal political and class conflicts in Japan.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Memo on a Soviet article on 73d Diet resistance to the Mobilization Bill: disputes claims of failed unity, calling opposition the self-defense of discredited parties facing a totalitarian state.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Moscow Despatch No. 1291

subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of a Soviet article from Khabarovsk analyzing political and economic conflicts within wartime Japan.
subfiles.from: Alexander C. Kirk, Counselor of Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.summary: Kirk sends A. Vergin's Khabarovsk article on Japan's internal conflict, contrasting compliant Diets with resistance to the Mobilization Bill and predicting a military anti-Soviet adventure defeated by the Red Army.
subfiles.title: Moscow Despatch No. 1291: 'Soviet Comment on Internal Conflict in Japan'

subfiles.about: Presents a Soviet Marxist critique of parliamentary opposition, economic strain, mass arrests, and imperialist aggression in Japan.
subfiles.from: A. Vergin, Tikhookeanskaya Zvezda (Pacific Star)
subfiles.summary: This Soviet article discusses parliamentary opposition in the 73d Japanese Diet against the General Mobilization Bill, highlighting a confrontation between Lieutenant Colonel Sato and deputies. The author argues that heavy military casualties, economic depletion, and resilient Chinese resistance under the Kuomintang-Communist united front have undermined the Japanese bourgeoisie's hopes for a swift victory. It documents internal repression including mass arrests of students and dissolution of the legal proletarian party Nihon Musanto, asserting that the military clique seeks war against the Soviet Union to forestall internal collapse.
subfiles.title: Article Translation: 'Internal Conflict in Japan' by A. Vergin in Pacific Star

subfiles.about: Summarizes and analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 2975 regarding the personalities and administrative machinery of the reconstituted Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 2975 on the reorganized Konoe Cabinet: a central China policy organ under Ugaki, Ikeda's business approach, and Kwantung Army influence through Itagaki.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 2975

subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive biographical and political analysis of the new ministerial appointees in the reorganized Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the background and significance of the new ministers appointed to the Konoe Cabinet, focusing on General Ugaki (Foreign Affairs), Seishin Ikeda (Finance and Commerce & Industry), General Araki (Education), and General Tojo (Vice Minister of War). He examines Ugaki's reconciliation with the military and prospects for assuming the premiership, Ikeda's efforts to coordinate financial controls while reassuring business, and Araki's role in ideological mobilization. The despatch concludes that the reshuffled Cabinet represents a victory for Konoe that strengthens the regime for a more vigorous continental offensive.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2975: 'Changes Within the Konoe Cabinet'

subfiles.about: Records an official clerical correction in the text of Tokyo Despatch No. 2975.
subfiles.from: Division of Communications and Records (DCR:MJP)
subfiles.summary: Records correction of Despatch No. 2975, page 5: 'Foreign Minister' changed to 'Finance Minister' at the Embassy's request.
subfiles.title: Division of Communications and Records Memorandum Correcting Despatch No. 2975

subfiles.about: Requests a textual correction on page 5 of Tokyo Despatch No. 2975.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Embassy asks David Salmon to change 'Foreign Minister' to 'Finance Minister' on page 5 of Despatch No. 2975 (May 31, 1938).
subfiles.title: Tokyo Embassy Memorandum for Mr. Salmon Requesting Correction to Despatch No. 2975
subfiles.to: David A. Salmon, Chief of Division of Communications and Records

subfiles.about: Reports Cabinet efforts to place non-military China affairs under civilian control and suggests opening comprehensive diplomatic discussions with Ugaki.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoe, Ugaki and Ikeda aim to take non-military China administration from the military via a 'China organ' and development companies, and to reduce friction with the US and Britain. He proposes an interview with Ugaki.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 399: Extension of Estimate on Cabinet Reconstruction and China Policy

subfiles.about: Furnishes comprehensive instructions and a detailed outline of American desiderata for Ambassador Grew's representations to Foreign Minister Ugaki.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Hull approves Ambassador Grew's proposal to confer with Foreign Minister Ugaki and sets forth detailed principles and specific American desiderata. Hull expresses concern that the proposed 'China organ' and development companies resemble the monopolistic system established in Manchuria. The instructions demand protection of American lives, restoration of property, non-interference with treaty and extraterritorial rights, maintenance of the Chinese Maritime Customs, preservation of the Shanghai International Settlement, and adherence to the Open Door policy.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 212: Instructions and American Desiderata for Tokyo Embassy

subfiles.about: Paraphrases Tokyo Telegram No. 399 regarding civilian governance of China affairs and conditions of Ugaki and Ikeda's appointments.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 399: Konoe, Ugaki and Ikeda aimed to remove China's economic and political control from the army through a China organ and development companies, easing friction with the US and Britain.
subfiles.title: Department of State Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 399

subfiles.about: Urges that diplomatic representations press Japan to adopt a more reasonable attitude toward civilians and American missionary institutions in China.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, United States Ambassador to China
subfiles.summary: Johnson, from Hankow, says Americans' position would improve if Japan treated civilians reasonably; American missions, hospitals and schools seem targeted for interference.
subfiles.title: Hankow Telegram No. 313 Regarding Treatment of American Interests and Civilians

subfiles.about: Reports private assurances from Ikeda and Kodama that development companies in China will observe the Open Door and avoid monopolistic practices.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Ikeda and Kodama assure that China development companies will not copy Manchurian monopolies and will uphold the Open Door. Grew remains skeptical but sees it as positive before his Ugaki talk.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 422: Assurances on the Open Door in North and Central China

subfiles.about: Informs Ambassador Grew that the State Department perceives no reason to delay his interview with the Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Cordell Hull)
subfiles.summary: State Department tells Grew it sees no reason to delay his planned conference with the Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Tokyo Authorizing Immediate Representations

subfiles.about: Confirms that the procedure and timing for Ambassador Grew's approach to the Foreign Minister appear opportune to the Department.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Cordell Hull / Stanley K. Hornbeck)
subfiles.summary: State Department confirms the timing and procedure Grew outlined for representations to the Foreign Minister appear fully opportune.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Tokyo Approving Timing of Representations

subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt in Hankow of Department Telegram No. 212 of June 25 to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, United States Ambassador to China
subfiles.summary: Johnson reports from Hankow receiving Department Telegram No. 212 of June 25 to Tokyo on July 1, 1938.
subfiles.title: Hankow Telegram No. 327 Acknowledging Receipt of Department Instructions

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet concerning instructions to repeat Department Telegram No. 212 to Hong Kong and Hankow.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference (124.946/78): Telegram No. 212 of June 25 to be repeated to Hong Kong and Hankow.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Distribution of Telegram No. 212

subfiles.about: Reports that chauvinist efforts to appoint Shiratori as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs were abandoned to protect relations with the United States and Britain.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports chauvinists' pressure to appoint Shiratori Vice Minister was thwarted by the Prime Minister to protect US-British relations; Horinouchi mentioned as ambassador to Washington.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 438 on Foreign Office Appointments

subfiles.about: Reports on Ambassador Grew's two-hour conference with Foreign Minister Ugaki presenting comprehensive American desiderata and specific grievances.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan (relayed via Shanghai)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports a two-hour July 4 interview with Ugaki setting out American desiderata in China, handing over a summary and a list of over 250 cases of Japanese damage to American rights.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram (via Shanghai No. 945): Report on Representations to Ugaki
